title: Yoked to One
subtitle: A sentence from a back office, a word in Matthew, and a yoke that is broken and replaced.
body_md:
---

## Exhibit A: The position.

In securities operations there is a sentence that sounds like a confession. *Justify the position.*

Outside the building it means defend yourself. Inside the building, to anyone who has read about a financial scandal, it sounds like fraud: a man over a ledger, making the numbers say what someone needs them to say.

It meant the opposite.

An account is a holding. So many shares of a stock, owned by someone, held somewhere. Every position on the screen had to be proved against what lay beneath it: the firm's trade record, the firm's own books, and the statement from the party actually holding the shares. Three records, kept by three different hands, with no reason to flatter one another.

Where the three agreed, the position stood. Where they didn't, the gap was called a break, and a break was never smoothed over. It was traced. To a trade never recorded. To a price entered wrong. To a fee nobody booked. To a settlement that failed overnight.

Some breaks had a gentler cause. A company merges, or changes its name, and the morning check against Bloomberg catches it. The shares have not moved. Only the description has. The fix is a new label on the same holding.

Then came the correcting entry, or sometimes a series of entries, and a paper trail an auditor could follow back to the source. Only after that was the position justified.

I was hired to do that, for more than four years.

Fraud bends the record toward what someone wants. Justification bends it toward what is. The shares sit where they sit, and nobody in that building ever asked them to move. The wrong entry stayed in the history. The corrections stood beside it. The balance was true.

The old law ran the same arithmetic. Deuteronomy, chapter nineteen, verse fifteen: "At the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established." The Hebrew for established is *yaqum*, from a verb that means to rise, to stand. A matter backed by enough independent witnesses stands up. So did a position backed by three records.

---

## Exhibit B: The word in Matthew.

> "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart: and ye shall find rest unto your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light."

I had to look up the word *yoke*. In my head it lived next to breakfast. It is spelled Y-O-K-E, and it is a wooden beam laid across the necks of two animals so they can pull a plow together. One beam. Two necks. The ox beneath it does not choose the field. The hand on the plow does.

A yoke is built for a matched pair. The law in Deuteronomy, chapter twenty-two, forbids plowing with an ox and a donkey together. The usual reading is that unequal strides pull a furrow crooked.

Jesus says take, and the yoke is already His. Already made. Already in use. Take is the person's verb, and the only one. The field, the pace, and the setting-right are His.

He says learn after, so the wearing comes first and the understanding follows. The Greek verb is *manthanō*, the root of the word disciple. To learn of Him is to be apprenticed to Him.

The word carried more than a plow. Two people who work as one are said to be yoked. Marriage is a yoke, and the Latin, *iugum*, gave English conjugal. A yoke is also the fitted panel across the shoulders of a shirt, the part that bears the weight so the rest of the cloth can hang. And it means oppression, a duty so heavy that freedom is gone. All of it in one word, spoken once.

That last meaning belongs to Peter. At the council in Jerusalem he calls the old system of earning a yoke "which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear." The question in Matthew was never yoke or no yoke. It was whose.

A neck holds one beam.

---

## Exhibit C: A word with no present tense.

The other yoke has a name. It is a noun, and it sits on the page like a stone. Justice. Heavy, finished, with no motion in it. Put it in the present tense and the grammar refuses. You do not justice a situation. You justify it.

The Latin shows the split. *Iustitia* is the state of being right, something waited for and handed down. *Iustificare* is to make right, and somebody is doing it. A printer knows the verb. To justify a column of type is to space every line until both margins stand straight. The words are not argued into place. They are set against an edge.

Justice is the first language, and it is learned early. A headline says someone was held accountable, or wasn't, and the verdict lands in the chest before the article is read. A video of a man getting exactly what he had coming is watched twice, because it feels like a scale settling. A driver cuts across three lanes, and the whole car goes quiet while a ruling forms. A dinner check arrives, and somebody starts doing the arithmetic out loud.

The relationships carry it longest. A private tally with a sentence of its own: *after everything I did for you.* A job that takes more hours than it returns calls the difference balance. Each runs the same books, then adds a line underneath: what can be done to put the wrong thing right, and who will do it.

The answer arrives fast. I will.

It is not a wicked system. It is the best an earthbound world has built to keep people from devouring one another. But it runs on partial evidence, so every settlement is temporary, and it hangs the whole load from one neck. Each person becomes auditor of everyone's books. God's included.

---

## Exhibit D: The gift.

Justice asks the world to fit the person. The measuring tape is the person's own, carried to the altar for Heaven to sign. Justification runs the other way. The person is set against the edge. Not argued. Set.

A contract can be signed while trust is dead. A verdict can arrive in someone's favor while the heart stays still. A won case settles the account outside and leaves the weather inside alone.

Paul builds the other account in order. Romans, chapter three, verse twenty-four: "Being justified freely by his grace." The Greek for freely means as a gift, without payment. Nothing is owed on the other side of the ledger.

Then chapter four, verses four and five, where the language turns to bookkeeping: "Now to him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace, but of debt. But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness."

Reckoned and counted are one Greek verb, *logizomai*. It is an accounting word. To enter a sum to an account. Wages for work are entered as debt, Paul says. Something owed. The other entry is made differently, and the verb in the middle of that second sentence is justifieth. It is in the present tense, and God is its subject. The noun with no motion in it has a verb here, and the verb is moving. The One who justifies is doing it now.

Then chapter five, verse one: "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." Justified first. Peace after. The next verse says where the person is left: "this grace wherein we stand." The Greek is in the perfect tense. A standing taken once, and still held.

The position stood. A matter established stands. Here it is a person.

---

## Exhibit E: The broken yoke.

The Old Testament has a story about a man who tried to live without one.

Jeremiah walked through Jerusalem wearing a wooden yoke on his neck, a sign that the nation would serve Babylon. A prophet named Hananiah took it off him and broke it in front of the crowd. He promised that within two years it would all be over.

Jeremiah went away, and the word came back. "Thou hast broken the yokes of wood; but thou shalt make for them yokes of iron."

A broken yoke gets replaced. Whether was never the question. What it would be made of was.

Wood. Iron. Egypt's. The old system of earning that Peter named. Every one of them is a yoke somebody puts on, and every one is carried alone.

Then, on a hillside, a different offer. *Take my yoke.*

The words themselves say whose it is. The yoke Christ names is the Father's. "I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me." He speaks of the Father's yoke, and He wears it first.

A heavy brace, a field, a pair of oxen. The gut tightens at the picture, and that is the ordinary response. The answer is in the pronoun. My yoke. Jesus is already under it.

The one who takes it is the unseasoned ox, paired to the seasoned one. The responsibility is shared, and so is the outcome. The glory goes to the Father, who created all things and maintains them. To be yoked to Jesus is to be yoked to the will of the Father. That is why easy and light are plain descriptions of the load, and not comfort.

The field is still a field.
